body_md: Every value has one **owner**. When owner goes out of scope, value is dropped. No GC, no manual free. This single rule eliminates double-free and leaks by construction.
hook: Rust has no garbage collector — yet memory frees itself perfectly.

quiz.q: How does Rust ensure heap memory like a String is freed safely without a garbage collector?
options: A runtime garbage collector periodically scans memory for unreferenced strings
The developer must manually call a free() or deallocate() function
The compiler automatically injects a drop call as soon as the owner variable exits scope
The memory stays allocated until the operating system shuts down the process
quiz.explain: Rust ties memory lifecycle to variable scope: when the owner leaves its enclosing scope, drop runs deterministically.

takeaway: Scope exit drops the owner and frees the value.
trap: Expecting GC timing; drop happens deterministically at scope end.

body_md: Assigning a `String` **moves** ownership — old variable becomes invalid. This prevents two owners freeing same heap data. Use-after-move is a compile error, not a crash.
hook: let b = a; kills a — the most shocking line for newcomers.

quiz.q: When you execute `let b = a;` where `a` is a heap-allocated String, what happens to `a`?
options: Both a and b share ownership of the same underlying heap buffer
Ownership moves to b, making a immediately invalid and unusable
a remains valid because Rust creates an implicit deep copy
The program panics with a double-free runtime exception
quiz.explain: In Rust, assignment of heap types moves ownership by default, preventing double-free bugs at compile time.

takeaway: Assignment of heap values moves ownership.
trap: Using moved value gives `borrow of moved value` error.

body_md: Passing a `String` to a function **moves** it unless you return it. Caller loses ownership. Take `String` only when function should consume the data.
hook: Calling a function can destroy your variable — by design.

quiz.q: When passing an owned String into a function fn take(s: String), what happens to the caller binding?
options: Ownership transfers into the function, so the caller can no longer use that variable
The caller retains full ownership and can freely access the string afterward
Rust automatically duplicates the string data on the stack for the function
The variable becomes global and accessible anywhere in the program
quiz.explain: Passing a value by value moves ownership into the callee; once called, the caller can no longer reference it.

takeaway: By-value params consume ownership.
trap: Passing String then reusing it fails; borrow with & instead.

body_md: `.clone()` makes a deep copy of heap data — slow but explicit. Only clone when you truly need two independent owners. Cloning in a loop kills performance.
hook: clone() fixes the compiler error — but seniors flinch when they see it.

quiz.q: What actually happens under the hood when you call s.clone() on a String?
options: It creates a fast pointer alias pointing to the existing memory buffer
It converts the heap string into a static compile-time string slice
It explicitly creates a full deep copy of the heap buffer with its own independent owner
It temporarily borrows the string for the duration of the current statement
quiz.explain: clone() performs an explicit deep copy of heap contents, giving both bindings independent memory at the cost of allocation.

takeaway: Clone duplicates data; use sparingly.
trap: Sprinkling clone to silence moves hides perf costs; prefer borrows.

body_md: Integers, floats, bool, char are `Copy` — assignment duplicates bits, no move. Types with heap data like `String` or `Vec` are never Copy. Custom types opt in with `#[derive(Copy, Clone)]`.
hook: Why do ints survive let b = a but Strings do not?

quiz.q: Why does `let b = a;` leave `a` fully usable when `a` is an i32, but not when it is a String?
options: Integers are stored in global registers, whereas strings are stored in thread-local storage
i32 implements the Copy trait (simple bitwise stack copy), while String manages heap resources
The compiler treats numeric variables as immutable constants that cannot be moved
Strings in Rust are reference-counted while numbers are garbage-collected
quiz.explain: Types with fixed stack sizes like i32 implement Copy, meaning assignments duplicate bits without transferring ownership.

takeaway: Stack-only primitives are Copy; heap types move.
trap: Assuming String is Copy; only Clone works and it is explicit.

body_md: `&s` **borrows** immutably — read without owning. Function gets a reference, caller keeps ownership. Most functions should take `&str` or `&T`, not owned values.
hook: Read data without owning it — the borrow is Rust's superpower.

quiz.q: When a function takes a borrowed reference `&s`, how does ownership behave between caller and callee?
options: The caller retains full ownership, granting the callee temporary read-only access
The callee claims ownership permanently and must return the reference to restore it
The data is copied to the callee stack frame for the duration of the call
The value is immediately deallocated once the callee finishes execution
quiz.explain: Borrowing with & allows read-only access without transferring ownership, leaving the caller in control.

takeaway: Borrow with & to read without taking ownership.
trap: Taking String by value when &str suffices forces needless moves.

body_md: Many borrows can coexist: `&T` is **shared**. Ten readers are fine because none can mutate. Data race impossible when mutation is impossible.
hook: Ten people can read the same book — as long as nobody writes in it.

quiz.q: How many immutable shared references (&T) can safely exist to the same data at the same time?
options: Only one reference at any given time
Up to two references, provided they are in the same scope
As many as you want simultaneously, since read-only readers cannot cause data races
Zero, unless the data is wrapped inside a mutex
quiz.explain: Any number of immutable borrows can coexist simultaneously because concurrent readers cannot mutate the underlying state.

takeaway: Unlimited shared borrows are allowed together.
trap: Thinking borrows are exclusive; only &mut is exclusive.

body_md: `&mut s` borrows **exclusively** for mutation. Only one active `&mut` at a time, and no `&` alongside it. Compiler enforces this aliasing rule.
hook: Only one writer allowed — Rust enforces it at compile time.

quiz.q: What restrictions does the borrow checker place on mutable references (&mut T)?
options: You can have multiple &mut references as long as they reside in different threads
Exactly one active mutable reference is allowed, with zero shared references active alongside it
Up to three mutable references are permitted within a single function body
Mutable references can coexist freely with any number of immutable references
quiz.explain: Rust guarantees memory safety by enforcing exclusive access: either one writer (&mut) XOR multiple readers (&).

takeaway: Mutable borrows are exclusive by design.
trap: Holding & while creating &mut gives `cannot borrow as mutable` error.

body_md: Borrow checker rule: **either many `&` or one `&mut`, never both**. Violation is compile error, catching data races before they run. NLL ends borrows at last use.
hook: The one borrow rule that kills 90% of data races.

quiz.q: What is the core aliasing rule enforced by the Rust borrow checker to prevent data races?
options: You may have unlimited mutable references, but only one immutable reference
You can have many immutable references simultaneously with one mutable reference
You may have either many shared readers (&T) OR one exclusive writer (&mut T), never both
References can only be created within loops or conditional match expressions
quiz.explain: Rust fundamental borrow rule is: many readers XOR one writer. This invariant eliminates data races at compile time.

takeaway: Many readers XOR one writer, enforced statically.
trap: Keeping a & alive (e.g. in println later) blocks &mut creation.

body_md: References must never outlive their data. Borrow checker rejects **dangling refs** via lifetimes. `fn dangle() -> &String` cannot compile — owned value drops at return.
hook: This 4-line function is impossible in Rust — and that saves you.

quiz.q: Why does the compiler refuse to build a function that returns a reference to a local variable (&String)?
options: The local variable is dropped at the end of the function, leaving a dangerous dangling pointer
Rust does not permit functions to return references under any circumstances
Returning references requires the unsafe keyword and raw pointer casting
The function must return an integer error code instead of a reference
quiz.explain: Local variables cease to exist when their enclosing function frame pops; returning their reference would create a dangling pointer.

takeaway: References can never outlive their referent.
trap: Trying to return &String from helper; return owned String instead.
output:
error[E0106]: missing lifetime specifier
// cannot return a reference to local `s` — return String instead

body_md: A **slice** `&[T]` or `&str` is a (pointer, length) view into data you do not own. `&s[0..2]` borrows part of a String. No copy, no ownership change.
hook: Borrow half a string without copying a single byte.

quiz.q: What does a slice like &str or &[T] actually represent in memory?
options: A newly allocated heap array containing a copy of the selected elements
A lightweight two-word fat pointer containing a memory address and a length
A cryptographic hash that dynamically maps keys to original values
A compressed byte stream that decodes lazily on iteration
quiz.explain: Slices are fat pointers: they store a pointer to the start of the data and the number of elements, without copying.

takeaway: Slices are lightweight borrowed views.
trap: Slicing mid-UTF8-char panics; slice on char boundaries only.

body_md: Prefer `&str` params over `&String`: they accept String, literals, and slices alike. Deref coercion makes `&String` act as `&str` at call sites automatically.
hook: fn f(s: &String) is almost always wrong — one character fixes it.

quiz.q: Why is &str strongly preferred over &String for function parameters that only read text?
options: &String requires manual heap allocations on every single function call
&str is faster to compile because it bypasses the type checker
&str flexibly accepts string literals, slices, and owned strings via automatic deref coercion
&String is deprecated in modern Rust editions and triggers compiler warnings
quiz.explain: &str is much more versatile: it accepts string literals (&static str), slices, and &String via deref coercion.

takeaway: Take &str for flexible read-only text APIs.
trap: Using &String params rejects literals and slices needlessly.

body_md: **Structs** bundle named fields. Use `struct Name { f: T }`, init with `Name { f }`, access with `.`. `..other` fills remaining fields via struct update syntax.
hook: Classes are gone — this simpler grouping replaces them.

quiz.q: How does Rust model custom composite data types containing multiple named, typed fields?
options: Using `struct Name { ... }` with named fields and explicit types
Using object-oriented `class Name extends Object { ... }`
Using runtime interfaces that dynamically resolve field names
Using procedural macros that generate global variable tables
quiz.explain: Structs bundle related named values together into a single cohesive, strongly typed data structure.

takeaway: Structs model data with named typed fields.
trap: Forgetting a field in literal errors; use ..base to fill rest.

body_md: Tuple structs `Name(T, U)` and unit structs `Name;` are compact variants. Good for newtypes like `Meters(f64)` that add type safety with zero cost.
hook: A struct with no field names? It is a power move for type safety.

quiz.q: How does the newtype pattern (struct Meters(f64)) improve code safety without adding runtime overhead?
options: It compresses 64-bit floats down into 32 bits at runtime
It creates a distinct, strongly checked type that prevents accidental mixing of identical primitive units
It converts runtime arithmetic into compile-time macros
It automatically validates that numeric values are greater than zero
quiz.explain: Wrapping a primitive in a single-field tuple struct creates a distinct compile-time type with zero memory overhead.

takeaway: Newtypes add safety with zero runtime cost.
trap: Forgetting .0 access on tuple structs; fields are positional.

body_md: **Enums** list variants a value can be: `enum Dir { N, S, E, W }`. Variants can hold data: `Some(T)`, `Ok(T)`, `Err(E)`. Use `::` to construct each case.
hook: An enum that carries data inside each option — no nulls needed.

quiz.q: What makes Rust enums far more expressive and powerful than traditional C or Java enums?
options: Rust enums are always mapped to 64-bit integer values
Each enum variant can optionally hold its own custom payload and data types
Enums can be dynamically modified and extended at runtime
Enum variants do not need to be declared before they are used
quiz.explain: Rust enums are tagged unions: each variant can be unit-like, a tuple, or a struct holding data.

takeaway: Enums encode choices plus their payloads.
trap: Treating enums like ints; use match, not == chains, to unpack.
output: // compiles clean, no output — c holds Coin::Penny

body_md: `match` must be **exhaustive**: handle every variant or add `_` wildcard. Each arm can bind payloads. Compiler warns if you miss a future variant.
hook: Forget one case and Rust refuses to build — future-you says thanks.

quiz.q: Why does the Rust compiler require pattern matching with `match` to be strictly exhaustive?
options: Exhaustiveness guarantees that every possible variant is handled, preventing unhandled state bugs
It allows the compiler to convert all match statements into fast binary search trees
It is a stylistic guideline enforced only when running cargo clippy
Non-exhaustive matches cause silent program termination with zero exit codes
quiz.explain: Exhaustive matching ensures no variant is overlooked, so adding a new enum variant prompts compile errors wherever it is used.

takeaway: Match exhaustively so new variants cannot slip through.
trap: Missing arm gives non-exhaustive pattern error; add _ or variant.

body_md: `if let` handles **one** interesting case, ignoring rest. Shorter than match for single-variant checks. Pair with `let-else` when you need early return on mismatch.
hook: Full match for one case is overkill — this cuts it to two lines.

quiz.q: When is using `if let Some(x) = expr` preferred over writing a full `match` expression?
options: When you only care about matching one specific variant and want to ignore all others cleanly
When you need to handle every possible variant with specialized error logic
When the expression being matched is an asynchronous future
When performance is critical, since if let skips pattern verification
quiz.explain: if let is concise syntactic sugar for matching a single pattern when all other cases can be ignored.

takeaway: Use if let for single-pattern checks.
trap: Using if let when you need exhaustive handling hides missed cases.

body_md: `Option<T>` is `Some(T)` or `None` — Rust's null replacement. No null derefs possible: you must handle None via match, `unwrap_or`, `?`, or combinators before use.
hook: Rust deleted null — and replaced it with something strictly better.

quiz.q: How does Option<T> eliminate the notorious billion-dollar mistake of null pointer exceptions?
options: It automatically supplies a fallback zero or empty string whenever null occurs
It forces developers to explicitly handle the None possibility before accessing the value
It turns null dereferences into non-fatal background warnings in the log
It replaces null pointers with heap-allocated sentinel strings
quiz.explain: In Rust, values cannot be null. Optional values must be wrapped in Option<T>, forcing explicit handling of absence.

takeaway: Option makes absence explicit and checkable.
trap: Calling unwrap blindly panics on None; prefer unwrap_or or ?.

body_md: Chain Options without nesting: `map` transforms Some, `and_then` chains fallible steps, `unwrap_or` supplies defaults. Keeps happy path flat and readable.
hook: Nested if-Some pyramids collapse into one clean line.

quiz.q: How can you transform the value inside an Option<T> without writing nested `match` statements?
options: By repeatedly calling .unwrap() inside a try-catch exception block
By casting the Option into a raw pointer and dereferencing it directly
By chaining functional combinators like .map() and .and_then()
By setting a global panic hook that catches missing values
quiz.explain: Combinators like map and and_then allow declarative, flat transformations of optional values without nested boilerplate.

takeaway: Combinators keep Option pipelines flat.
trap: Using map where and_then needed nests Option<Option<T>>.

body_md: `Result<T, E>` is `Ok(T)` or `Err(E)` for recoverable errors. `match`, `?`, or combinators handle it. Unlike exceptions, error path is visible in the type signature.
hook: Errors as values, not explosions — the signature tells the truth.

quiz.q: Which standard Rust type represents an operation that can either succeed with data or fail with a recoverable error?
options: Option<T>
panic::Catch<T>
Result<T, E>
std::error::Null<T>
quiz.explain: Result<T, E> encodes either success (Ok(T)) or failure (Err(E)), making recoverable errors part of the type signature.

takeaway: Result makes errors part of the API contract.
trap: Ignoring Err with let _ hides failures; handle or propagate.

body_md: Methods take `self`, `&self`, or `&mut self` in `impl` blocks. `&self` reads, `&mut self` mutates, `self` consumes. Call with dot: `rect.area()`.
hook: No this, no self confusion — three receivers cover every case.

quiz.q: Which method receiver should you specify when a method only needs to read instance fields without modifying or consuming it?
options: &self (borrows the instance immutably for reading)
&mut self (borrows the instance exclusively for mutation)
self (takes full ownership and consumes the instance)
Self (calls a static constructor on the type)
quiz.explain: &self borrows the instance immutably, allowing caller code to reuse the struct after calling the method.

takeaway: Pick receiver by ownership need: borrow, mutate, or consume.
trap: Using self when &self suffices moves the value unexpectedly.

body_md: Associated functions like `String::new()` have no self — call on type itself. Constructors are just convention: `fn new(...) -> Self`. No `new` keyword needed.
hook: There is no new keyword — yet constructors still exist.

quiz.q: How do constructors work in Rust given that there is no `new` keyword in the language?
options: Constructors are defined using special compiler annotations
They are plain associated functions (commonly named new) that return Self
Objects are instantiated by calling dynamic factory methods provided by the runtime
The compiler automatically generates default zero-initialized constructors for all structs
quiz.explain: In Rust, constructors are just conventional associated functions defined inside impl blocks that return Self.

takeaway: Constructors are plain associated functions returning Self.
trap: Writing p.new() instead of P::new() confuses instance vs type call.
output: // compiles clean, no output — p holds P { x: 5 }

body_md: `#[derive(Debug)]` auto-implements printing with `{:?}`. Add `Clone`, `PartialEq` similarly. Derives remove boilerplate for common traits instantly.
hook: One line above your struct writes code for you.

quiz.q: What is the idiomatic way to enable debug formatting ({:?}) on a custom struct without manual implementation?
options: Write an explicit impl std::fmt::Display block by hand
Cast the struct to a string slice before calling println!
Annotate the struct definition with #[derive(Debug)]
Include the struct inside a tuple struct with a printable field
quiz.explain: #[derive(Debug)] instructs the compiler to generate the formatting boilerplate automatically.

takeaway: Derive common traits instead of hand-writing them.
trap: Forgetting Debug derive then using {:?} fails with formatting error.

body_md: Field init shorthand: `User { name, age }` when variables match field names. Destructuring `let User { name, age } = u;` unpacks similarly. Less repetition, fewer typos.
hook: Stop writing name: name — Rust already knows what you mean.

quiz.q: When can you use Rust field init shorthand syntax like `User { name, age }`?
options: Whenever local variable names exactly match the struct field names
Only when all fields are primitive integer or boolean types
Exclusively inside unit test functions and integration modules
Whenever the struct implements the Default trait
quiz.explain: When local variables share the exact names of struct fields, you can omit the field: value repetition.

takeaway: Use field shorthand to cut boilerplate.
trap: Shadowing a field name then using shorthand binds wrong value.

body_md: Use `let-else` to extract from Option/Result or **diverge** early: `let Some(x) = v else { return; }`. Guarantees x valid after, no nesting, no unwrap.
hook: Unwrap without panicking and without nesting — meet let-else.

quiz.q: How does `let Some(val) = opt else { return; };` simplify extracting values from an Option?
options: It panics automatically if the option is None
It binds val in the outer scope on success, or executes an early diverging return branch
It retries the operation in a background thread until a value becomes available
It converts the option into an uninitialized raw memory buffer
quiz.explain: let-else provides clean guard syntax: it unwraps and binds variables in the outer scope or diverges immediately.

takeaway: let-else flattens fallible extraction with early exit.
trap: Else branch must diverge (!); plain fallback value will not compile.
